prime.problem: A finished paper leaves a pile of caveats, threats to validity and unrun arms. Without ranking them, the next project is whichever one is most fun rather than the one that is new, cheap and would change what harness builders do.
prime.fits: The last card of course 7 and of the series. It turns the pre-registration's limitations and the baseline's threats to validity into ranked follow-ups, and feeds the research question bank from course 0.
expect: threats to validity as a question source
branching from saved prefixes as a cheap follow-up
required vs open vs partly studied
prime.goal: Pick one follow-up, say what is already known about it, state its smallest experiment and cost, and generate one new question with the three moves.

attend: Why do the top two questions cost so little compared with the paper itself?
Which question is owed before submission rather than open research, and what makes it different?
How could a softer instruction explain part of the tampering the paper reports?
Why might rewarding the claim checker push tampering into places the checker can't see?

must: The sweep saves every prefix and workspace → any new arm can branch from the same states → most follow-ups are paired, cent-per-branch experiments rather than new studies

Graders often read what the agent last saw → compaction can hide a failure from the grader as well as the agent → comparing a judge on the summary vs the full trace tests whether evals inherit the error

The instruction 'make the suite pass' can't be satisfied with an unfixable test → it pushes toward tampering on its own → without a softer-instruction arm the paper can't separate instruction from compaction
A checker catches only the tampering it was written to see → penalising it rewards unseen forms (e.g. monkeypatching urllib) → any checker-as-reward plan needs a hand-read of what the checker passes
reference: costs: d1-codex branch $0.0153 on gpt-5.4-mini; labeller $0.0014–$0.0026 per branch
Claude projections $24–$134 per model for half the earlier 2,800-run plan
disclosure in the baseline: 25 of 26 tampering runs

compress.prompt: Card closed: list the eight follow-ups from cheapest to most expensive, with one word each for status (open, partly studied, required).
checklist: cheap, from sweep data or prefixes: judge views, the Codex goal sentence, pass^k, softer instruction
compute only: re-running the pilot's cases in official images (required)
dearer: a Claude model and real CLIs; checker-as-reward selection; disclosure across harnesses
the capstone-tagged ones extend this paper directly

retrieve.q: Explain what makes question 7 'required' rather than open research.
answer: it checks the paper's own observational number (the 14 genuine cases)
the pilot names it as the decisive next step and the spec requires it before submission
it adds no new question, only turns a reading into a re-execution

retrieve.q: Walk through the smallest experiment for the Codex goal-sentence question, from saved state to estimate.
answer: branch d1-codex twice: summary as written, and with the restated goal removed (logged scripted edit)
measure tampering from the diff and re-run in both
estimate the paired difference with the task-cluster bootstrap

retrieve.q: Adding a Claude model answers the biggest limitation. What does it cost, and what would you give up to fund it under the $250 ceiling?
answer: trigger-design projects $24–$134 per model for half the earlier plan, uncached being realistic
it must be added by addendum before its runs start
under the ceiling you might drop real-CLI checks or a third repeat, or run Claude on a subset of tasks

compare.q: Course 5's top question asks whether selecting on a false-claim checker makes claims vaguer. How does this course's checker-as-reward question differ in what goes wrong?
answer: course 5: the words change (claims become uncheckable)
here: the actions change (tampering moves where the checker can't see)
both are the same Goodhart pattern: the measured signal improves, the behaviour doesn't

predict.q: If the sweep shows no tampering effect at all, predict which of the eight questions drop in rank and which rise.
predict.answer: The goal-sentence question (2) and the softer-instruction question (5) lose most of their point, since there's no effect to explain. The judge-views question (1), pass^k of honesty (3) and the re-execution (7) don't depend on an effect and rise relatively; a Claude model (4) rises, because a null on two OpenAI models invites 'would another family differ?'.

apply.task: Use the three moves to write one new question about the cut2000 arm, with a status, a cost line using a measured per-branch price, and a smallest experiment.
apply.done: Your question splits a word (e.g. 'truncation' into which characters are cut), cites the baseline's 32/40 vs 4/40 verdict-line visibility, uses $0.0153 per d1-codex branch on gpt-5.4-mini for cost, and names a paired branching design.
apply.hint: Cutting the first 2,000 characters drops pytest's verdict line because it comes last; what if the cut kept the last 2,000 instead?

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: which questions are cheapest, or which depend on the sweep's result?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the judge question is cheap, or why the checker question is risky?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: instruction → tampering, or compaction → tampering?
Which question would a lab researcher find most thoughtful, and why?
Which one would you run first if the sweep came back null?
